October 15, 2026 - Dex Horthy w/ contributions from Gabe Orlanski NOTE: This is Part I of our October 2026 writeup: the Q4 state of the slop. Gabe and the SlopCodeBench team will share their analysis and a more qualitative deep dive into slop patterns in Part II. For my previous writeups on SlopcodeBench, see benchmarking-opus-5-on-slop-code-bench.md and benchmarking-sol-fable-kimi-on-slop-code-bench.md . Both include deeper dives on the core structure of SCB and how each of its challenges is broken into checkpoints. In May, the last time SCB was published, gpt-5.5 got a 14.8% strict pass rate on slopcodebench . This month, I ran the frontier models through the same campaigns, and the highest scorer was gpt-6 astra, hitting 16.3% . While the benchmark reports several different pass rates, the one we focus on is strict pass rate - in how many checkpoints did the model pass every test case while still passing all regression tests the frontier models we tested here had strict pass rates in the 12.2-16.3% range: For comparison, the benchmark also reports a "core pass rate" which is less strict, which lands in the 65.8-74.0% pass rate for these models. One interesting thing here that I'll dig into - medium effort performed better than XHigh for some newer models. XHigh costs 2.11-4.22x as much as Medium in the three complete pairs, and most notably, opus 5.5 did BETTER on medium effort than on xhigh Over the past few months, I ran subsets of the bench. I started with three problems , then tried six . This time: 36 problems and 196 checkpoints per setting . Since we used a subset before, we can't use the earlier subsets to measure improvement or decline. The full benchmark lets us compare these results with the official research findings. It also means while the 30% fable 5 score from the latter of those two is interesting, its not comparable here, because it only covers 6 out of 36 problems. SlopCodeBench gives a coding agent a problem in stages. It writes a program, gets new requirements, and changes the existing code. Later checkpoints test both new behavior and old behavior. The idea here is that this maps more onto how software is really built - with unclear and evolving requirements during the course of the build. For folks who want to try to repro these findings: I used the pinned v1.0 catalog, the stock just-solve prompt, seed 42, the any-case runner pass policy, and Docker with Python 3.12 and uv. I ran each model and effort setting once. Each checkpoint builds on the code from earlier checkpoints. Some problems have more checkpoints than others. Each checkpoint counts equally toward the pass rate, so problems with more checkpoints have more weight. Strict passes: 24-32 of 196. Core passes, including strict: 129-145. The tinted portion isn't extra strict success. Astra XHigh has the most strict passes in this snapshot. But it's lead over SOL 6.1 Medium is only two checkpoints . Opus Medium leads Core success at 145/196 , but passes only 28/196 strictly. XHigh costs more in all three pairs; strict success rises only for Astra. These single runs don't isolate effort as the cause. This doesn't prove that more reasoning hurts coding. It says higher effort was not a reliable way to buy more strict passes in these runs . One campaign per setting can't tell me how much is run-to-run variation. Recorded estimates span $178.51-$1,550.07 within a 12.24-16.33% strict-score range. GPT-6.1 Medium has the lowest recorded cost at $178.51, with the same strict count as Astra Medium. Fable's recorded estimate is about 8.68x as much, with three fewer strict passes. Checkpoint success also isn't the same as ending with a working program. Only each problem's last checkpoint counts here. Failed test cases aren't distinct bugs; skips stay separate. First - the models left a ton of junk and scratch code while working. My first reaction was to remove the random temp files from the quality scores. But I chatted with gabe and he made a good point: the benchmark should measure how much garbage models leave in the codebase. If we're not reading the code, we need to measure it. Tests, scratch code, and generated copies probably shouldn't get a free pass just because they aren't the main program. I did use a fixed list of folder names to exclude installed packages, virtual environments, and caches from both analyses. The main results analyze all leftover code. For comparison, we also calculate the same metrics after removing a fixed list of temporary and generated files. That lets us see how much the cleanup changes the numbers. The rules and the actual difference are below. These figures cover the same 28 problems for all ten completed runs , not all 36 problems. The scanner couldn't fully measure some files in eight problems (more on that in gabe's update later), so we left those problems out for every model. Some high level details on how we compute "what % of this code triggers at least one slop rule": We total the flagged lines and source lines across all 28 problems, then divide to get the percentage. Larger programs therefore have more weight. In the earlier posts, we averaged each problem's percentage instead. Opus XHigh has the lowest slop percentage at 77.75% , versus 94.25% for Opus Medium. Interestingly, once again, the xhigh version has fewer strict passes: 25 versus 28. It is possible that this is because newer models come with new / different slop patterns, and the paper's original battery of 200+ linters is focused on a set of hand-curated patterns derived from agent-authored PRs in the months preceding the original publication in march 2026 and the v1.1 in may 2026. These new models may produce new maintainability anti-patterns that we haven't built linters for yet (more on that in Gabe's follow up post). Opus Medium leaves the most code, even after filtering. We don't remove all tests. For the filtered score, we leave out folders named _work , tmp , temp , scratch , generated , build , or dist , plus *_pb2.py and *_pb2_grpc.py files. We use the same rules for every run. We don't guess whether code looks generated or exclude tests as a group. In these runs, the filter only removed _work files: 45 files and 41,265 source lines , all from Opus Medium's final dynamic_buffer code. Its total drops from 216,881 to 175,616 source lines , and slop-presence drops to 92.90% . It still ranks most-frequent on slop presence. The filter changes nothing for the other models. Fable has the lowest mean complexity, 3.57; GPT-6 SOL Medium has the highest, 11.70. Functions and methods each get one vote. As you might expect, splitting code into more helper functions can lower average complexity without making the code easier to change. Less code isn't always better either. There's a ton more metrics and I'm excited to get Gabe's take on the more qualitative side of these outputs. The full benchmark is hard in a way that matters to me: the agents get the main behavior right much more often than they keep all tested behavior working as requirements change. We're getting better at maintaing a codebase over time (14.8% to 16.3% during may->september), but not as fast as anyone would have you believe. I think we'll be keeping the lights on for a while to come. NOTE: This is Part I of our October 2026 writeup: the Q4 state of the slop.
